transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-01-24 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Jamal Bryant (Redwood Solutions), Dana Sato (Sunward CTO), Omar Khalid (ML Eng), Priyanka Rao (Infra Lead), Ben Ortiz (Product), Maya Chen (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy):
Sunward is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for a real-time nav assistant -- main constraints: p95 <= 250ms for short responses (50-120 tokens) during steady traffic, worst-case burst spikes to 400 concurrent streams with streaming token rates of ~30-50 tokens/sec per stream. They care about region residency, audit logs, and KMS/HSM. Interested in a trial and a benchmarking run.

Topics:
- p95 targets and how Redwood measures them
- concurrency and multiplexing / batching tradeoffs
- streaming token/sec benchmarking approach and sample scripts
- hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC) performance considerations
- compliance: SOC 2, KMS, audit logs, SSO

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll do quick intro then jump to their constraints — Dana, want to kick off with what you're trying to achieve?
[00:12] Dana Sato: Sure. Hi all. We're building a live navigation assistant inside the cockpit UI, so latency is critical. For short prompts like route updates and confirmation strings we need p95 under 250ms ideally. For longer system summaries it's okay to be a little higher.
[00:28] Marco Ruiz: Got it. When you say p95 at 250ms, is that end-to-end from client to token streaming first byte, or server-side generation time?
[00:36] Dana Sato: End-to-end, including network where possible. Our front-end measures time-to-first-token as the user-perceived latency.
[00:44] Marco Ruiz: Ok that's helpful. Typical quick question — what's your average sequence length for those fast replies?
[00:51] Omar Khalid: Usually 30 to 80 tokens for confirmations, 120 to 300 for summaries. Our model is a fine-tuned 13B open model, currently quantized to int8 and running in house for experiments.
[01:04] Priyanka Rao: And infra-wise we have k8s on GCP, VPC, private subnets. We need to know if Redwood Private (on-prem/VPC) will match hosted latency or if Dedicated is a better fit.
[01:16] Lena Park: Good. Let's break it down. There are three levers here: model size/quantization, runtime kernels and batching, and networking/region placement. For real-time p95 we often recommend dedicated capacity pinned to lower batch sizes + streaming mode to minimize time-to-first-token.
[01:35] Ben Ortiz: Can you unpack that — dedicated vs hosted differences in p95?
[01:40] Marco Ruiz: Yeah. Hosted offers our global catalog and is easiest to spin up — but shared pools can cause variance under noisy neighbors. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and deterministic performance; you'll get tighter p95s. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you complete network control, but there are ops tradeoffs.
[01:58] Dana Sato: So for our 250ms p95 on 30–80 tokens, what kind of throughput per GPU are we talking about?
[02:06] Marco Ruiz: Roughly, for a 13B int8 on a modern A100-equivalent in our runtime, a single GPU can serve around 15–25 concurrent streaming clients hitting the short path with small batch sizes while keeping p95 in the 150–300ms window. But that number changes a lot with seqlen and token/sec.
[02:26] Omar Khalid: That seems low — we're expecting spikes up to 400 concurrent streams during peak events.
[02:32] Marco Ruiz: Understood — that's where pooling and autoscaling come in. For sustained 400 concurrent streams, you'd likely need a pool of 20–30 GPUs depending on exact token rates, batching tolerance and prefix caching. We typically model this from your token/sec distribution.
[02:47] Lena Park: Also, prefix/KV caching can reduce cost and latency if many requests hit similar prompts — do you have repetitive prompts?
[02:55] Ben Ortiz: Yes, many are templated confirmations so ~40% are repeats per session.
[03:01] Maya Chen: Security question — we need KMS integration. If we go Dedicated, can we use our Cloud KMS or an HSM? We also need audit logs retention for 12 months.
[03:11] Marco Ruiz: Yes, Dedicated and Private support customer KMS (Cloud KMS) and we have HSM integrations for Private in many cases. Audit log retention is configurable as an add-on; we can store logs in your bucket or a managed retention store. We'll share the SOC 2 + encryption docs.
[03:27] Dana Sato: What's the typical p95 delta between hosted and dedicated? Like numbers we can model.
[03:33] Marco Ruiz: In our benchmarks we've seen hosted p95 for small responses around 180–400ms p95 depending on noisy neighbor variance, whereas dedicated often lands in 110–220ms range for similar workloads. Streamed responses can shave a bit if you reduce the first-token latency. But again, model size & quantization matter.
[03:51] Omar Khalid: What about cold start behavior? If a fleet scales up from 10 to 30 GPUs rapidly, do we see p95 spikes during the scale period?
[03:59] Marco Ruiz: Yes, cold-starts exist. That's why we provide burst capacity and pre-warming options. We also have fallback policies — route to a slightly smaller model or a cached response during scale events. Those are tradeoffs you can configure in rollout policies.
[04:13] Lena Park: Can we talk about the streaming token/sec number you mentioned? They called out 30–50 tokens/sec per stream, is that sustained?
[04:21] Omar Khalid: On spikes yes, sustained for a minute or so per session, especially when users ask for multi-sentence summaries while driving.
[04:29] Marco Ruiz: If each stream is 30–50 tokens/sec and you have 400 concurrent streams sustained, that's 12k–20k tokens/sec aggregate. We model both tokens/sec and concurrency to size GPU pools. With batching and continuous KV cache we can get very good throughput but it increases latency. So you tune batching (delay window) vs p95.
[04:49] Ben Ortiz: What's an example tradeoff point? Like if we accept p95 of 350ms could we reduce GPU count by 30%?
[04:57] Marco Ruiz: Ballpark — yes, relaxing p95 from 250ms to 350ms can allow larger micro-batches and cut cost by ~20–40% depending on seqlen and model. We'll run a cost/latency curve for your traffic.
[05:12] Priyanka Rao: For the benchmarking run, what inputs do you need from us?
[05:17] Marco Ruiz: We'll need: a representative traffic trace (timestamps + token lengths), the model artifact or model name, desired p95 target(s), region preference, and any security requirements. We'll run a baseline test on hosted and on a dedicated trial cluster to show deltas.
[05:30] Omar Khalid: We can't share the full dataset — can you run a synthetic trace?
[05:33] Marco Ruiz: Yep. We can run synthetic traces that match your token length and tokens/sec distributions. It's ideal if you can give percentiles: p50/p95 payload sizes and expected burst profile.
[05:44] Dana Sato: Is there a quick way to see impact of quantization? We're already on int8 but considering int4.
[05:50] Marco Ruiz: Int4 often reduces memory and improves throughput but can change quality. Redwood Optimize includes quantization recommendations per workload; for latency we can benchmark int4 vs int8 on a dedicated node.
[06:02] Maya Chen: Are there network tweaks you recommend? We need TLS and private subnets, but anything on keepalive or proxying that helps first-byte latency?
[06:10] Marco Ruiz: Keepalives and long-lived connections are critical for streaming. In Private/VPC deployments you avoid public egress hops which helps. We also recommend colocating model hosts in the same region as your app edge to cut RTT.
[06:24] Ben Ortiz: Can you share a sample token/sec streaming script?
[06:28] Marco Ruiz: Yes — we'll push a repo with a streaming harness that gradually ramps connections and emits tokens at configurable rates. That will be in the benchmark package I send.
[06:38] Lena Park: Ok let's capture next steps now — Marco will prepare the script and run a baseline on a 1 GPU instance to show per-stream latency numbers. Dana/Priyanka will provide traffic percentiles. We'll share compliance docs.
[06:52] Omar Khalid: One more — fallback policies. If we route to a smaller model during peak, how do you manage semantic parity? We can't have contradictory responses in safety-critical nav hints.
[07:02] Marco Ruiz: You can configure strict fallback chains, and Redwood Optimize can run evals on your prompt set to score regressions. For safety-critical flows you can mark routes as non-fallback so they always hit the high-fidelity model with higher cost.
[07:17] Maya Chen: Great. And SSO? We use Okta, need SAML and RBAC.
[07:22] Jamal Bryant: Okta SAML and fine-grained RBAC are supported for Dedicated and Private; hosted supports SSO for the console and API keys for service accounts. We'll include RBAC docs.
[07:31] Dana Sato: Awesome. Any rough timeline for a trial?
[07:34] Lena Park: If we get the traffic sample today, Marco can spin a 1-GPU baseline by Friday, and we can stand up a dedicated trial cluster early next week pending procurement.
[07:45] Ben Ortiz: Procurement — do you have a standard MSA or PO flow?
[07:48] Lena Park: We have standard enterprise terms; for Dedicated/Private we'll do quote + MSA. Jamal will follow up on procurement workflow.
[07:58] Marco Ruiz: I'll note one caveat — if you request strict time-to-first-token p95 <150ms at 13B without aggressive queuing, that usually pushes toward multi-region edge or more GPUs. We'll show tradeoffs in the report.
[08:12] Dana Sato: Good call out. Ok let's wrap.
